about.html: About SubtitleFixer SubtitleFixer is a set of free subtitle tools that run entirely in your browser, so your files never leave your device. You can shift subtitle timings, fix garbled characters, and convert between SRT, VTT and ASS without creating an account or uploading anything. Who it's for SubtitleFixer is for anyone whose subtitles don't quite work, for example: The subtitles appear too early or too late compared to the speech. The text shows strange characters like Ã© , Ð¿Ñ€Ð¸ or � instead of normal letters. Your player or website needs a different format, like VTT instead of SRT. You don't need to know anything about encodings or subtitle formats. Pick the tool that matches your problem, drop in your file, and download the fixed version. Why everything runs in your browser SubtitleFixer processes your subtitle files on your own device, not on a server. When you add a file, the page reads it and fixes it with code running in your browser. The file is not sent anywhere, so there is nothing to upload, nothing to wait for, and nothing stored on our side. We built it this way because: Privacy: subtitles can be personal or unreleased work, and you shouldn't have to hand them to a stranger's server. Speed: small text files are fixed instantly, with no upload or download queue. Simplicity: no account, no sign-up, no email address. The tools Shift subtitles – Move all subtitle timings earlier or later by a number of milliseconds, optionally starting from a specific cue, in SRT, VTT or ASS files. Fix subtitle drift – Re-time subtitles that start in sync but slowly drift: set the correct time for two lines and every cue is corrected, or use a frame-rate preset (23.976↔25, 24↔25 or 23.976↔24 fps). Fix subtitle encoding – Automatically detect the file's encoding, preview a few possible readings, choose the one that looks right for your language, repair double-encoded text (mojibake like Ã© instead of é ), and save it as UTF-8, with an optional BOM for older players. SRT to VTT – Convert one or more SubRip (.srt) files to WebVTT (.vtt), the format used by HTML5 video. VTT to SRT – Convert one or more WebVTT (.vtt) files back to SubRip (.srt). ASS to SRT – Convert Advanced SubStation Alpha (.ass) and SubStation Alpha (.ssa) files to SRT by removing styling tags (italics and bold are kept as <i> and <b> ), turning \N into real line breaks, and merging duplicate lines from multiple layers. If you process one file, you download it as a file. If you process several files at once, you download them together as one zip. How SubtitleFixer is funded SubtitleFixer is free to use, and there is no paid version. If a tool saved you some time, you can leave an optional tip through Ko-fi . Donations are never required, and every tool works the same whether you donate or not. Contact Found a bug, a file that doesn't convert properly, or have an idea for a new tool? Email luntovskiy.k.a@gmail.com . SubtitleFixer is run by Kirill Luntovskii. See also: Privacy policy
ass-to-srt.html: How to convert ASS to SRT in 3 steps You can convert ASS to SRT in three steps, and your files stay on your device the whole time. Add your ASS or SSA files. Drag one or more .ass or .ssa files onto the page, or click to choose them. Convert. SubtitleFixer removes the styling tags, keeps italics and bold as and , turns \N into line breaks and merges duplicate layers. Download. One file downloads as an SRT file; several files download together as one zip. Example: before and after The ASS lines below have styling tags, an italic word, a \N line break and the same line on two layers. Before (ASS file, [Events] section): [Events] Format: Layer, Start, End, Style, Name, MarginL, MarginR, MarginV, Effect, Text Dialogue: 0,0:00:05.37,0:00:08.12,Default,,0,0,0,,{\an8}Where are we going?\NTo the {\i1}station{\i0}. Dialogue: 0,0:00:09.00,0:00:11.45,Default,,0,0,0,,{\blur4\bord6}I'll wait here. Dialogue: 1,0:00:09.00,0:00:11.45,Default,,0,0,0,,I'll wait here. After (SRT file): 1 00:00:05,370 --> 00:00:08,120 Where are we going? To the station. 2 00:00:09,000 --> 00:00:11,450 I'll wait here. The {\an8} and {\blur4\bord6} tags are gone, the italic tags became and , \N became a real line break, and the line that was on two layers is now one subtitle. The times are exactly the same, written with three digits for the milliseconds. What it does and doesn't do The converter keeps the dialogue and timing of your ASS subtitles and removes everything SRT can't show. What it does: Converts ASS and SSA (Advanced SubStation Alpha and SubStation Alpha) files to SRT. Removes styling tags such as {\an8} , {\blur4} or {\pos(…)} . Keeps italics and bold: {\i1} … {\i0} becomes … and {\b1} … {\b0} becomes … . A tag left open is closed at the end of the line. Turns \N and \n into real line breaks and \h into a normal space. Skips Comment: lines and removes drawing events (vector shapes drawn with {\p1} ). Detects the file's encoding and saves the SRT file as UTF-8. Tick "Add BOM (old players)" if your device needs a BOM. Merges lines with the same start, end and text (after tags are removed) into one SRT subtitle. Keeps signs and song lyrics as normal subtitle lines. Keeps every start and end time exactly. Converts several files at once, with one zip to download. Runs in your browser: your files never leave your device, and there's no sign-up. What it doesn't do: It doesn't keep fonts, colours, positions, karaoke or animations. SRT can't store them, so signs and songs appear as plain lines in the usual subtitle position. It doesn't repair double-encoded text like Ã© . Use Fix subtitle encoding for that, where you can compare previews and pick the right reading. It doesn't fix subtitles that are out of sync. Use Shift subtitles , which also works directly on ASS files. It doesn't convert SRT to ASS. When to keep ASS instead of converting Keep the ASS file if the styling matters and your player supports it; convert to SRT if your device or app needs SRT. ASS is common for anime and fansubs, where signs, songs and on-screen text are placed and styled carefully. Players like VLC and mpv show all of that. After converting to SRT, every line, including signs and songs, appears in the usual subtitle position, with only italics and bold kept. Convert to SRT when: your TV, streaming box or media server app doesn't show ASS subtitles properly, a video editor or website only accepts SRT, you just want readable dialogue without effects. For a full comparison of the formats, read SRT vs VTT vs ASS . Related tools Fix subtitle encoding : for subtitles that show Ã© , Ð¿Ñ€Ð¸ or other garbled characters. Shift subtitles : for subtitles that appear too early or too late, in SRT, VTT or ASS files. SRT to VTT converter : turn SRT subtitles into VTT for web video players. VTT to SRT converter : turn VTT captions into an SRT file. Guide: SRT vs VTT vs ASS . Fix subtitle drift FAQ What do I lose when I convert ASS to SRT? You lose fonts, colours, positions, karaoke effects, animations and vector drawings, because SRT can't store them, so the ASS tags and drawing lines that create them are removed. The timing, the text, and italics and bold (as and ) are kept. Will the dialogue and timing stay exactly the same? Yes. ASS stores times in hundredths of a second and SRT in thousandths, so 0:00:05.37 in an ASS file becomes 00:00:05,370 in the SRT file with no rounding. The dialogue text stays the same, minus the styling tags. Why do some converters give me duplicate lines? ASS files often place the same line on two or more layers, for example once for a soft outline and once for the text on top. A simple converter turns each copy into its own SRT subtitle, so every line appears twice. SubtitleFixer merges lines with the same start time, end time and text (after the tags are removed) into one subtitle. Are italics and bold kept? Yes. SubtitleFixer turns {\i1} … {\i0} into … and {\b1} … {\b0} into … , and closes any tag left open at the end of the line. All other styling tags, such as fonts, colours and positions, are removed. What's the difference between ASS and SSA? SSA (SubStation Alpha) is the older format, and ASS (Advanced SubStation Alpha) is the newer version with more styling options. Both work the same way here: drop the .ass or .ssa file and get an SRT file back. My ASS subtitles show garbled characters. How do I fix that? The converter detects the encoding of your ASS file automatically and always saves the SRT file as UTF-8, so files saved in an older encoding are read on the way. If the result still shows characters like Ã©, the text was probably double-encoded: repair it with Fix subtitle encoding , which accepts .ass and .ssa files, then convert. How do I export SRT from Aegisub? In Aegisub, go to File → Export Subtitles, click Export, and choose SubRip (*.srt) as the file type. If you only have the .ass file and no Aegisub, you can convert it here instead. Is my ASS file uploaded? No. SubtitleFixer converts ASS to SRT inside your browser, and your file never leaves your device. There is no upload and no sign-up.
fix-subtitle-drift.html: How to fix subtitle drift in 3 steps You can fix subtitle drift in three steps, and your file stays on your device the whole time. Add your subtitle file. Drag an SRT, VTT or ASS file onto the page, or click to choose it. Two-point sync works on one file at a time; frame rate presets can convert several files at once. Set the correct time for two lines. The first and last lines are selected by default; you can pick any other two from the list. For each one, type the time it is actually spoken in the video, as hh:mm:ss,mmm (for example 01:28:25,480 ). If you know both frame rates, you can pick a preset such as 25 → 23.976 fps instead. Download the fixed file. Every line is re-timed to match, the text stays the same, and the file keeps its format. Example: before and after In this SRT file the subtitles are 1 second late at the start and about 3 minutes 40 seconds late by the end. Before: 1 00:00:50,000 --> 00:00:52,500 Is anyone there? 612 00:45:10,250 --> 00:45:13,000 We should have left an hour ago. 1204 01:32:05,500 --> 01:32:08,750 It's over. Let's go home. While watching the video, you note that line 1 is spoken at 00:00:49,000 and line 1204 (the last line) at 01:28:25,480 . You enter those two times for the two lines that are selected by default. After: 1 00:00:49,000 --> 00:00:51,400 Is anyone there? 612 00:43:22,840 --> 00:43:25,480 We should have left an hour ago. 1204 01:28:25,480 --> 01:28:28,600 It's over. Let's go home. You only set lines 1 and 1204. Line 612, and every other line, moved into place on its own. In this example every time was multiplied by 0.96 and then moved 1 second later, which is what a 24 fps vs 25 fps mismatch plus a 1-second offset looks like. What it does and doesn't do This tool fixes subtitles that get gradually further out of sync. It does not fix a sudden jump in the middle of a file. What it does: Re-times every line from two lines whose correct time you set: the first and last line, or any two lines. Fixes gradual drift and a constant delay at the same time. Converts subtitle frame rates with presets for 23.976 ↔ 25, 24 ↔ 25 and 23.976 ↔ 24 fps, for one file or several at once (several files download as one zip). Works with SRT, VTT and ASS files, keeps the format and keeps the text as it is. Rounds every new time to a whole millisecond. Runs in your browser: your file never leaves your device, and there's no sign-up. What it doesn't do: It doesn't fix subtitles that are fine up to one point and then suddenly jump, for example after a cut scene. Use Shift subtitles and start the shift from the line where the jump happens. It doesn't watch the video or find the right times for you. You enter the correct times for the two lines yourself. It can't change subtitles inside streaming services like Netflix, Disney+ or YouTube. It only works on subtitle files you have on your device. Presets cover 23.976, 24 and 25 fps. For any other mismatch, use two-point sync. How two-point sync works Two-point sync uses the two times you enter to work out a straight-line correction for the whole file. Think of the subtitle timeline as a rubber band. SubtitleFixer stretches or squeezes it until the distance between your two lines is right, then slides it until both lines sit in the right place. Every other line moves along with it. In math terms, each time t becomes a × t + b . Here a is the stretch (for example 0.96) and b is the slide (for example +1 second). You don't need to calculate either one: SubtitleFixer works them out from your two lines. For the best result, choose two lines that are far apart and easy to hear, such as short lines of dialogue near the start and near the end. Subtitle frame rate converter: 23.976 ↔ 25 fps The frame rate presets re-time subtitles made for one frame rate so they match a video with another, without entering any times. A frame rate mismatch is a common reason for drift. Many European TV and DVD releases play films at 25 fps, which is about 4% faster than the 23.976 fps used by most Blu-ray and web releases. Subtitles made for one version slowly drift against the other: by almost 4 minutes over a 90-minute film. Between 23.976 and 24 fps the difference is only 0.1%, which is still about 5 seconds over 90 minutes. Each preset is labelled "subtitle fps → video fps": the first number is the frame rate the subtitles were made for, and the second is the frame rate of your video. 23.976 fps here means the exact NTSC film rate, 24000/1001, and new times are rounded to whole milliseconds. Preset Every time is multiplied by Pick it when the subtitles appear… 23.976 → 25 fps ≈ 0.9590 later and later 25 → 23.976 fps ≈ 1.0427 earlier and earlier 24 → 25 fps 0.96 later and later 25 → 24 fps ≈ 1.0417 earlier and earlier 23.976 → 24 fps ≈ 0.9990 slowly later and later 24 → 23.976 fps 1.001 slowly earlier and earlier Example with the 25 → 24 fps preset (every time × 25 ÷ 24). Before (subtitles made for 25 fps): 1 00:00:04,800 --> 00:00:07,200 Good morning. 640 00:48:00,000 --> 00:48:02,400 Did you hear that? After (matching a 24 fps video): 1 00:00:05,000 --> 00:00:07,500 Good morning. 640 00:50:00,000 --> 00:50:02,500 Did you hear that? At the start the change is only 0.2 seconds, but by line 640 it is 2 minutes. That growing gap is why a single shift can't fix a frame rate mismatch. To check your video's frame rate in VLC, go to Tools → Codec Information. If you don't know the frame rate the subtitles were made for, use two-point sync instead. Presets work in batch: add several files, such as every episode of a season, and download them together as one zip. Two-point sync handles one file at a time, because each file needs its own two lines. Related tools Shift subtitles : for subtitles that are off by the same amount all the way through, or that jump at one point. Fix subtitle encoding : for subtitles that show Ã© , Ð¿Ñ€Ð¸ or other garbled characters. SRT to VTT converter : turn SRT subtitles into VTT for web video players. VTT to SRT converter : turn VTT captions into an SRT file. ASS to SRT converter : turn styled ASS subtitles into a plain SRT file. Guide: Subtitles out of sync: shift vs drift . FAQ Why do my subtitles start in sync and then drift further off? The subtitles were timed for a version of the video that plays at a slightly different speed, often because of a different frame rate such as 25 fps instead of 23.976 fps. The difference between those two is about 4%, which adds up to almost 4 minutes by the end of a 90-minute film. How do I know whether it's drift or a constant delay? Check how far off one line near the start is, then one line near the end. If both are off by about the same amount, it's a constant delay and you can use Shift subtitles . If the gap is clearly bigger at the end, it's drift, and this page fixes it. How does two-point sync work, and which two lines should I pick? You pick two lines from the list and type the time each one is actually spoken, and SubtitleFixer works out how much to stretch the whole timeline and how far to slide it so both lines land in the right place. The first and last lines are selected by default; if they aren't clear dialogue, pick two other short lines that are far apart. Should I convert 23.976 to 25 fps or 25 to 23.976 fps? If the subtitles appear later and later compared to the speech, use 23.976 → 25. If they appear earlier and earlier, use 25 → 23.976. If you're not sure, use two-point sync, which doesn't need frame rates at all. How do I find my video's frame rate? In VLC, open the video and go to Tools → Codec Information, where the video track shows its frame rate. You don't need to know the frame rate of your subtitles if you use two-point sync instead of a preset. Do I need two-point sync or a frame rate preset? Use a frame rate preset if you know both frame rates and the subtitles are right at the very start. Use two-point sync if you don't know the frame rates or the subtitles are also shifted, because it fixes drift and a constant delay at the same time. Presets can convert several files at once, for example a whole season; two-point sync works on one file at a time. Does fixing drift change the text or the length of each line? The text stays exactly the same. Each line's length is stretched or squeezed by the same small factor as the timeline, so with a factor of 0.96 a line that lasted 2.5 seconds now lasts 2.4 seconds. Is my subtitle file uploaded? No. SubtitleFixer fixes subtitle drift inside your browser, and the file never leaves your device. There is no upload and no sign-up.
fix-subtitle-encoding.html: How to fix subtitle encoding in 3 steps You can fix garbled subtitles in three steps, and your file stays on your device the whole time. Add your subtitle file. Drag an .srt, .vtt, .ass, .ssa, text-based .sub or .txt file onto the page, or click to choose it. Pick the version that reads correctly. SubtitleFixer detects the encoding and shows 3–4 previews side by side. If none looks right, choose your subtitle language. If you see patterns like Ã© or Ð¿Ñ€Ð¸ , pick the repaired double-encoding version. Download it as UTF-8. The BOM is off by default; tick "Add BOM (old players)" only if your device needs it (see below). One file downloads as it is; several files download together as one zip. Example: before and after This Russian SRT file was saved as Windows-1251 but read as Western text, so every letter turned into a Latin symbol. Before: 1 00:00:03,200 --> 00:00:05,600 Ïðèâåò! Êàê äåëà? After (read as Windows-1251, saved as UTF-8): 1 00:00:03,200 --> 00:00:05,600 Привет! Как дела? This French SRT file was double-encoded: it was already UTF-8, but it was read as Windows-1252 and saved again. Before: 14 00:01:12,040 --> 00:01:14,500 Le cafÃ© est trÃ¨s bon. After (double encoding repaired): 14 00:01:12,040 --> 00:01:14,500 Le café est très bon. In both examples only the characters changed. The numbers, timestamps and line breaks are exactly the same. What it does and doesn't do This tool changes how the text in your subtitle file is stored. It does not change the timing or the words. What it does: Detects the encoding automatically and shows 3–4 possible readings side by side. Lets you choose your subtitle language to get a better guess. Accepts SRT, VTT, ASS, SSA, text-based SUB and TXT files. Reads common older encodings, including Windows-1251, Windows-1252, Windows-1254, Windows-1256, the ISO-8859 family (including ISO-8859-8 for Hebrew and ISO-8859-9 for Turkish), Shift_JIS and GB18030. Repairs double-encoded text (mojibake), such as Ã© → é , as a separate option in the preview. Saves the result as UTF-8, with an optional BOM, and changes nothing else in the file. Runs in your browser: your file never leaves your device, and there's no sign-up. What it doesn't do: It can't bring back letters that were already replaced by ? or � in the file. That information is gone, so you need a new copy of the subtitles. It doesn't fix boxes (□) that appear because your device has no font for that language. That's a player or font problem, not a file problem. It doesn't change timings. For that, use Shift subtitles or Fix subtitle drift . It doesn't translate subtitles. Why subtitles show weird characters Subtitles show weird characters when the file was saved in one encoding and your player reads it in another. An encoding is the rule that turns letters into bytes. UTF-8 covers every language, but many subtitle files, especially older ones, use a local encoding such as Windows-1251 for Cyrillic or Windows-1256 for Arabic. The bytes are fine; they are just being read with the wrong rule. Reading the file with the right encoding and saving it as UTF-8 fixes it for good. Mojibake: when text is encoded twice Mojibake from double encoding happens when a UTF-8 file is read as Western text (Windows-1252 or Latin-1) and then saved again. Each accented or non-Latin letter becomes two or three odd characters, often starting with Ã , Â , â or Ð . SubtitleFixer looks for these patterns and offers a repaired version as a separate option in the preview. You see It should be Typical language Ã© é French, Spanish, Portuguese Ã¨ è French, Italian Ã¼ ü German, Turkish ÃŸ ß German â€™ ’ (curly apostrophe) English and many others Ð¿Ñ€Ð¸ при Russian The repair works because the original bytes are still there, just misread. It can't work if the characters were replaced by ? along the way. Encodings by language The right encoding usually depends on the language of the subtitles. Language Encodings older files often use Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian (Cyrillic) Windows-1251 Arabic, Persian Windows-1256 French, German, Spanish, Portuguese and other Western European languages Windows-1252, ISO-8859-1 Greek ISO-8859-7 Turkish Windows-1254, ISO-8859-9 Hebrew ISO-8859-8 Japanese Shift_JIS Chinese (Simplified) GB18030 (which also covers GBK and GB2312) You don't need to know the encoding yourself. Choose your language, compare the previews, and keep the one that reads correctly. UTF-8 with or without BOM A BOM (byte order mark) is an invisible marker at the very start of a file that says "this file is UTF-8". Without BOM: fine for most modern players, TVs, websites and video editors. With BOM: helps some older players and TVs that otherwise guess the wrong encoding. SubtitleFixer saves without a BOM by default. Tick Add BOM (old players) if your device still shows garbled text after the fix. A BOM doesn't change the text or the timings. Related tools Shift subtitles : for subtitles that appear too early or too late by the same amount. Fix subtitle drift : for subtitles that get further out of sync over time. SRT to VTT converter : turn SRT subtitles into VTT for web video players. VTT to SRT converter : turn VTT captions into an SRT file. ASS to SRT converter : turn styled ASS subtitles into a plain SRT file. FAQ Why are my subtitles showing weird characters like Ã© or â€™? The file was saved in one encoding and is being read in another. For example, Ã© is the letter é saved as UTF-8 but read as Western (Windows-1252) text. Choosing the right reading and saving the file as UTF-8 fixes it. Why do Arabic, Persian, Cyrillic or Hebrew subtitles turn into gibberish? These subtitles are often saved in an older, language-specific encoding, such as Windows-1256 for Arabic and Persian or Windows-1251 for Cyrillic. A player that expects a different encoding shows text like ÇáÓáÇã or Ïðèâåò instead. Pick your language, choose the preview that reads correctly, and save it as UTF-8. How do I convert an SRT file to UTF-8? Add the SRT file, choose the preview where the text reads correctly, and download it. SubtitleFixer saves the result as UTF-8, without a BOM unless you tick "Add BOM (old players)". What is mojibake, and can it be reversed? Mojibake is garbled text such as Ã© instead of é or Ð¿Ñ€Ð¸ instead of при, which happens when UTF-8 text is read with the wrong encoding and saved again. It can usually be reversed, and SubtitleFixer offers the repaired text as a separate option in the preview. It can't be reversed if the characters were already replaced by question marks. Should I save my subtitles with a UTF-8 BOM? Only if your player or TV needs it. Most modern players read UTF-8 without a BOM, so SubtitleFixer leaves it off by default, but some older players and TVs only recognise UTF-8 when the BOM is there. If the file still looks garbled on your device, save it again with "Add BOM (old players)" ticked. The automatic detection picked the wrong encoding. Can I choose another? Yes. SubtitleFixer shows 3–4 possible readings of your file side by side, so you can pick the one that looks right. Choosing your subtitle language also helps it make a better guess. Why do my subtitles work in VLC but not on my Smart TV? VLC can guess the encoding or use one you set (Tools → Preferences → Subtitles / OSD → Default encoding), but many TVs can't. Saving the subtitles as UTF-8 gives the TV a standard encoding to read, and ticking "Add BOM (old players)" can help older models. Is my file uploaded, and does fixing the encoding change the timing? No to both. SubtitleFixer fixes the encoding inside your browser, so your file never leaves your device. Only the characters change (plus the optional BOM); the timings, line breaks and everything else stay exactly as they were.
guides/srt-vs-vtt-vs-ass.html: SRT files are the simplest and most widely supported, VTT files are the standard for video on the web, and ASS files are for styled, positioned subtitles. This guide explains what each format is, compares them side by side, shows the same lines in all three, and tells you which one to use for YouTube, websites, Plex, Jellyfin and VLC. What is an SRT file? An SRT file is a plain-text subtitle file in the SubRip format: numbered cues, each with a start time, an end time and one or more lines of text. Each cue has four parts: a number, a timing line with --> between start and end, the text, and a blank line. Times use hours, minutes, seconds and milliseconds, with a comma before the milliseconds. 1 00:00:01,500 --> 00:00:04,000 Is anyone here? 2 00:00:04,200 --> 00:00:06,800 Over here! By the window. SRT subtitles have no header, no styles and no positioning. Some players understand simple HTML-like tags such as for italics, but support varies. Some DJI drones also write a .srt file next to each video. That file holds flight and camera data, not dialogue. What is a VTT file? A VTT file is a WebVTT (Web Video Text Tracks) subtitle file, the format that HTML5 video uses for subtitles and captions. A VTT file must start with the line WEBVTT . Times use a dot before the milliseconds, and the hours can be left out when they are zero. Cue numbers are optional. After the timing, you can add cue settings that control position and alignment. WEBVTT 00:00:01.500 --> 00:00:04.000 Is anyone here? 00:00:04.200 --> 00:00:06.800 line:10% align:start Over here! By the window. Here, line:10% moves the second cue near the top of the video and align:start aligns its text to the start of the line. WebVTT also supports , and tags, voice tags like , NOTE comments and CSS styling through STYLE blocks or the page's own CSS. What is an ASS file? An ASS file is an Advanced SubStation Alpha subtitle file, which stores subtitles together with styles, positions and effects. An ASS file is split into sections. [Script Info] holds general settings, [V4+ Styles] defines named styles (font, size, colors, outline, alignment), and [Events] holds the subtitle lines. Each line starts with Dialogue: and lists its layer, start and end time, style and text. Times use one digit for hours and hundredths of a second. [Script Info] ScriptType: v4.00+ PlayResX: 1920 PlayResY: 1080 [V4+ Styles] Format: Name, Fontname, Fontsize, PrimaryColour, SecondaryColour, OutlineColour, BackColour, Bold, Italic, Underline, StrikeOut, ScaleX, ScaleY, Spacing, Angle, BorderStyle, Outline, Shadow, Alignment, MarginL, MarginR, MarginV, Encoding Style: Default,Arial,56,&H00FFFFFF,&H000000FF,&H00000000,&H80000000,0,0,0,0,100,100,0,0,1,2,1,2,40,40,40,1 [Events] Format: Layer, Start, End, Style, Name, MarginL, MarginR, MarginV, Effect, Text Dialogue: 0,0:00:01.50,0:00:04.00,Default,,0,0,0,,Is anyone here? Dialogue: 0,0:00:04.20,0:00:06.80,Default,,0,0,0,,{\an7\i1}Over here!{\i0}\NBy the window. In the last line, {\an7} places the text at the top left, {\i1} and {\i0} switch italics on and off, and \N is a line break. ASS override tags can also set exact positions ( \pos ), movement ( \move ), rotation, fades and karaoke timing ( \k ). SSA (SubStation Alpha) is the older version of the same format. ASS (v4.00+) added layers, transparency and rotation, and uses [V4+ Styles] instead of [V4 Styles] . SRT vs VTT vs ASS: comparison table The main differences are the header, the timing syntax, and how much styling and positioning each format can hold. Choose the format based on where the subtitles will play, and use the simplest one that does what you need. For SRT files, only basic files work: YouTube ignores styling, and the file must be plain UTF-8. For VTT files, YouTube supports positioning, but styling is limited. ASS files are not on YouTube's list of supported formats, so convert them with the ASS to SRT converter first. HTML5 video The HTML element loads subtitles and captions in WebVTT format, so use a VTT file. A browser won't read an SRT file there: the WebVTT parser rejects any file that doesn't start with WEBVTT . Convert with the SRT to VTT converter . Plex Plex's help lists SRT, SMI, SSA/ASS and WebVTT as fully supported, both embedded in the video and as separate files. It also recommends saving text subtitles as UTF-8. An SRT file is the simplest choice. Keep an ASS file if you want its styling. A separate subtitle file should use the video's file name plus a language code, for example Movie Title (2020).en.srt next to Movie Title (2020).mkv . Jellyfin Jellyfin's documentation lists SubRip (SRT), WebVTT and ASS/SSA as text subtitle formats. It also warns that subtitles can cause transcoding: if a device can't show a subtitle format, the server may convert it or burn it into the video, and burning in is the most CPU-heavy kind of transcoding. If you don't need styling, an SRT file is the simplest choice. If you keep an ASS file, check that it plays well on the devices you use. VLC VLC plays all three. Its feature list includes SubRip and SSA text subtitles, and VLC 3.0 rewrote its WebVTT support, including CSS styling. Pick the format based on where else you'll use the file. What you lose when converting Converting to a simpler format keeps the text and timing but drops whatever the simpler format can't store. SRT file → VTT file: the text and timings carry over. The converter adds the WEBVTT header, drops the cue numbers (they're optional in VTT) and changes the commas in the times to dots. Simple tags like , and exist in both formats and are kept. VTT file → SRT file: the text and timings carry over. Cue settings (position, alignment, size), STYLE blocks, regions and NOTE comments have no equivalent in SRT subtitles, so they are lost. SubtitleFixer keeps , and , turns voice tags like into "Anna: " in front of the line, and removes YouTube tags and other tags. ASS file → SRT file: the text and timings carry over. Styles, fonts, colors, positions, karaoke and other effects are lost. SubtitleFixer keeps italics and bold as and , and signs and songs become normal subtitle lines. ASS files store hundredths of a second and SRT files store milliseconds, so the times convert exactly. Keep the original file if you might need the styling later. Save subtitles as UTF-8 Saving subtitle files as UTF-8 avoids most problems with garbled characters. The WebVTT standard requires UTF-8. YouTube asks for SRT files in plain UTF-8, and Plex recommends UTF-8 for text subtitles. If your subtitles show characters like Ã© or Ð¿Ñ€Ð¸ instead of normal letters, the file was saved or read in the wrong encoding. Use fix subtitle encoding to detect the right encoding and save the file as UTF-8, with or without BOM. SubtitleFixer's converters also detect the encoding of the file you add and always save the result as UTF-8. VTT to SRT converter : turn one or many VTT files into SRT files. ASS to SRT converter : turn styled ASS files into SRT subtitles, keeping italics and bold. Timing problems instead? See Subtitles out of sync: shift vs drift . Sources SubRip format: Library of Congress, SubRip Subtitle format (SRT) WebVTT: W3C, WebVTT: The Web Video Text Tracks Format and MDN, the element ASS: Aegisub, ASS override tags YouTube: Supported subtitle and closed caption files Plex: Adding local subtitles to your media Jellyfin: Codec support VLC: VLC features and VLC 3.0 release notes FAQ What's the difference between SRT and VTT? Both are plain-text subtitle formats with millisecond timing. A VTT file (WebVTT) must start with a WEBVTT line, uses a dot before the milliseconds (00:00:01.500) and supports positioning and CSS styling. An SRT file (SubRip) has no header, numbers every cue, uses a comma (00:00:01,500) and has no positioning. Should I use an SRT or VTT file for YouTube? YouTube accepts both. An SRT file is the simplest choice: YouTube reads basic SRT files in plain UTF-8, without styling. Use a VTT file if you need to position captions, since YouTube supports WebVTT positioning but only limited styling. Which subtitle format is best for Plex, Jellyfin or VLC? Plex, Jellyfin and VLC all support SRT, VTT and ASS files. An SRT file is the simplest and most predictable choice. Keep an ASS file when its styling matters to you. On Jellyfin, subtitles your device can't handle may be burned into the video, which takes a lot of server CPU. What is an ASS subtitle file, and when should I keep it instead of converting it to an SRT file? An ASS file (Advanced SubStation Alpha) stores subtitles with named styles and override tags for fonts, colors, positions and effects. Keep it when the styling carries meaning, such as translated signs or karaoke. Convert it with the ASS to SRT converter when your player or platform only takes plain subtitles. What is the difference between ASS and SSA? SSA (SubStation Alpha, v4) is the older format. ASS (Advanced SubStation Alpha, v4.00+) is its successor and adds features such as layers, transparency and rotation. ASS files use a [V4+ Styles] section, SSA files a [V4 Styles] section. Which conversion loses data? Converting an SRT file to VTT keeps the text and timings. Converting a VTT file to an SRT file drops positioning, style and region blocks and comments, because SRT subtitles have no place for them. Converting an ASS file to an SRT file drops styles, fonts, colors, positions and effects but keeps the text and timings; the ASS to SRT converter also keeps italics and bold as and . Can I just rename .srt to .vtt? No. A VTT file must start with the line WEBVTT and use a dot, not a comma, before the milliseconds. Without the header, browsers reject the file. Use the SRT to VTT converter instead. What is an SRT file, and how do I open it? An SRT file is a plain-text subtitle file in the SubRip format. You can open it in any text editor to read or edit it. To watch it with a video, give it the same name as the video file (for example movie.mp4 and movie.srt) and open the video in your player.
guides/subtitles-out-of-sync.html: Out-of-sync subtitles almost always have one of three causes: a constant offset, drift, or errors in one part of the file. Each one needs a different fix, so the first step is to find out which one you have. This guide shows you how to check, how to fix the subtitle file for good, and when a quick setting in your player is enough. Why are my subtitles out of sync? Subtitles go out of sync when the subtitle file was timed for a slightly different version of the video than the one you're playing. A subtitle file is just text with a start and end time for each line. It doesn't know which video it's playing with. If it was made for another release, the times no longer match what you see and hear. This happens a lot with downloaded movies and TV episodes, where the subtitles and the video often come from different sources. There are three typical patterns: Constant offset. Every line is early or late by the same amount, from the first minute to the last. A different intro, logo or recap at the start is a common cause. Drift. The subtitles are almost right at the start but get further off as the video plays. The usual cause is a frame-rate mismatch between the release the subtitles were made for and your video. Cue-level errors. Most of the file is fine, but the timing jumps after a certain scene, or a few single lines are wrong. Common causes are a different cut (for example extended vs theatrical) or ad breaks removed from a TV recording. How to tell which problem you have Check the sync at three points: near the start, in the middle and near the end of the video. Find a clearly spoken line near the start. Note how early or late its subtitle is. Do the same around the middle. Do the same near the end. Then compare what you found: What you see Problem What to do The same gap at the start, middle and end Constant offset Shift subtitles by that amount A small gap at the start, a bigger one in the middle, the biggest at the end Drift Fix subtitle drift with two-point sync Early at the start but late by the end, or the other way round Drift plus an offset Fix subtitle drift with two-point sync In sync until one scene, then off by a fixed amount Cue-level error (different cut or ad break) Shift subtitles starting from the first wrong line Only a few random lines are wrong Cue-level error (badly timed lines) Fix those lines in a subtitle editor, or find a file made for your release Constant offset: every line is off by the same amount A constant offset is fixed by moving every subtitle by the same number of milliseconds. To find the amount, compare when you hear a line with when its subtitle appears: If the subtitle appears after the voice, the subtitles are late. Move them earlier. If the subtitle appears before the voice, the subtitles are early. Move them later. For example, if a subtitle shows up 2 seconds after the line is spoken, move all subtitles 2,000 ms earlier. A quick way to measure is your player's subtitle delay setting (see player delay vs fixing the file ). Adjust it until the lines match, note the value, then apply the same amount to the file. To fix the file permanently, use shift subtitles . It moves every cue earlier or later by the number of milliseconds you enter, and it works with SRT, VTT and ASS files. Drift: the gap grows as the video plays Drift means the subtitle timing runs at a slightly different speed than the video, so no single shift can fix it. If you shift drifting subtitles to match the start, they'll be wrong at the end. If you match the end, the start will be wrong. The most common cause is a frame-rate mismatch: Films are usually shot at 24 frames per second, and many video releases use 23.976 fps. European PAL TV and DVD releases often play the same film at 25 fps, so it runs slightly faster and finishes sooner. Subtitles timed for one version drift against the other. Because 25 ÷ 23.976 ≈ 1.043, the timing is off by about 4%. That adds up to several minutes by the end of a feature film. To correct drift, use fix subtitle drift . It gives you two options: Two-point sync: enter the correct time for two lines, ideally one near the start and one near the end. Every cue is then re-timed in proportion. This fixes drift and any offset at the same time. Frame-rate presets: if you know both frame rates, convert directly between 23.976 and 25, 24 and 25, or 23.976 and 24 fps. Presets can convert several files at once, such as a whole season; two-point sync works on one file at a time. If you don't know the frame rates, use two-point sync. It works from what you actually see on screen. Cue-level errors: only part of the file is off When only part of the file is out of sync, fix that part on its own instead of the whole file. Different cut or removed ad breaks. The subtitles are in sync up to a certain scene, and everything after it is off by the same amount. Use shift subtitles and start the shift from the first line that's wrong. Lines before it stay as they are. If the timing jumps again later, repeat the shift from the next wrong line. A few badly timed lines. If only single lines appear too early or too late, no automatic tool can know the right time for each one. Fix those lines by hand in a subtitle editor, or look for a subtitle file made for your exact release. Missing or extra scenes. Subtitles for dialogue you never see, or long silent gaps where people are talking, point to a different cut. A subtitle file made for your version is usually the quickest fix. Player delay vs fixing the file A subtitle delay setting in your player is a quick fix for watching, but it doesn't change the subtitle file. That's fine if you only want to watch once. But if you play the file in another app, on another device, or share it, the problem comes back. Player delay settings also move all lines by the same amount, so they can't correct drift. For a permanent fix, change the file itself with shift subtitles or fix subtitle drift . VLC In VLC, press H or G during playback to change the subtitle delay. According to VLC's hotkey list, H turns the subtitle delay up and G turns it down. If the gap gets bigger, press the other key. This changes playback in VLC only. Your subtitle file stays the same. Plex Many Plex apps have an Adjust Offsets option in the playback settings. Plex's help says it works only for external text-based subtitles, such as a separate SRT file, and not for subtitles embedded in the video or image-based subtitles. Plex also has an Auto-Sync Subtitles option, which needs the server to analyse the video's audio first. Both are player settings: they don't edit your subtitle file. Jellyfin Jellyfin's web player has a Subtitle Offset option in the playback settings menu for text-based subtitles, such as SRT or VTT files. It isn't available for image-based subtitles like PGS. It adjusts playback only. The subtitle file stays the same. Streaming on Netflix, Prime Video or Hulu? SubtitleFixer can't fix subtitles on streaming services like Netflix, Prime Video or Hulu, because the subtitles aren't a file on your device. Our tools fix subtitle files that you have. Streaming apps load their own subtitles, and there's nothing for you to download and edit. What you can do: Check other titles. If every show is out of sync, the problem is probably your app or device. Restart the app or the device, and install any updates. Report the title. If only one show or movie is affected, report it to the service. Netflix, for example, lets you report a problem with a title from Viewing Activity in your account. FAQ Why are my subtitles out of sync? Your subtitle file was most likely timed for a slightly different version of the video. A different intro, a different frame rate or a different cut all change when each line should appear, and the subtitle file can't adjust to that by itself. How can I tell if my subtitles are offset or drifting? Check one clearly spoken line near the start, one in the middle and one near the end. If the subtitles are off by the same amount at all three points, it's a constant offset. If the gap grows from start to end, it's drift. Why do my subtitles get further out of sync the longer the video plays? That is drift. The subtitle timing runs at a slightly different speed than your video, usually because the file was made for a release with a different frame rate, such as 25 fps instead of 23.976 fps. A single shift can't fix it. Use fix subtitle drift instead. Does changing the subtitle delay in VLC change the subtitle file? No. The H and G keys in VLC change the subtitle delay for playback in VLC only. The subtitle file stays the same. To fix the file itself, apply the same delay with shift subtitles . Why are my subtitles right at first but wrong after a certain scene? Your video is probably a different cut, or ad breaks were removed from a TV recording. Everything after that point is off by the same amount. Use shift subtitles and start the shift from the first line that's wrong, so the earlier lines stay as they are. How much should I shift my subtitles? Compare when you hear a clear line with when its subtitle appears. If the subtitle shows up 2 seconds after the voice, move the subtitles 2,000 ms earlier. If it shows up before the voice, move them later. A player's subtitle delay setting is a handy way to find the exact value first. Should I fix timing before or after converting to another format? Either order works for a simple shift, because shift subtitles works with SRT, VTT and ASS files directly. The easiest approach is to fix the timing in the format you already have, then convert if you need to. Can I fix out-of-sync subtitles online for free? Yes. The SubtitleFixer timing tools are free and run in your browser. Your subtitle file is not uploaded, and you don't need an account.

shift-subtitles.html: How to shift subtitles in 3 steps You can shift subtitles in three steps, and your file stays on your device the whole time. Add your subtitle file. Drag an SRT, VTT or ASS file onto the page, or click to choose it. You can add several files at once, and they all get the same shift. Enter the shift in milliseconds. Use a positive number to make the subtitles appear later and a negative number to make them appear earlier. 1 second is 1000 ms. The ±100, ±500 and ±1000 buttons change the number in quick steps. To shift only part of the file, also enter the line to start from. Download the fixed file. It keeps the same format as the original. One file downloads as it is; several files download together as one zip. Example: before and after In this SRT file every line appears 2.5 seconds after it is spoken, so the shift is -2500 ms . Before: 1 00:00:12,400 --> 00:00:15,100 Where were you last night? 2 00:00:15,600 --> 00:00:18,250 I told you. I was at work. 3 00:01:03,980 --> 00:01:06,020 Nobody at work has seen you all week. After shifting by -2500 ms: 1 00:00:09,900 --> 00:00:12,600 Where were you last night? 2 00:00:13,100 --> 00:00:15,750 I told you. I was at work. 3 00:01:01,480 --> 00:01:03,520 Nobody at work has seen you all week. Every start and end time moved 2.5 seconds earlier. The text, the order and the length of each line stayed the same. What it does and doesn't do The shift tool moves subtitle timings by a fixed amount. It does not change the text or fix other kinds of timing problems. What it does: Moves every subtitle earlier or later by the same number of milliseconds. Starts the shift from a line you choose, if you want, and leaves the earlier lines alone. Works with SRT, VTT and ASS files and keeps the original format. Shifts several files at once by the same amount and gives you one zip to download. Removes lines that would end at or before 00:00:00 and trims lines that would start before it, tells you how many lines were removed or trimmed, and renumbers SRT files 1, 2, 3… Runs in your browser: your file never leaves your device, and there's no sign-up. What it doesn't do: It doesn't fix drift, where the subtitles get further off as the video plays. For that, use Fix subtitle drift . It can't change subtitles inside streaming services like Netflix, Disney+ or YouTube. It only works on subtitle files you have on your device. It doesn't work out the delay for you. You measure it once (see below). It doesn't fix garbled characters like Ã© . For that, use Fix subtitle encoding . Constant shift vs drift A constant shift means every subtitle is off by the same amount, from the first line to the last, and this page fixes exactly that. Drift is different: the subtitles are almost right at the start and clearly off by the end, because the gap keeps growing. A common cause is subtitles made for a version of the video with a different frame rate, such as 25 fps instead of 23.976 fps. Shifting can't fix drift, because no single number is right for the whole file. To tell them apart, check two lines: Check a line near the start of the video and note how far off it is. Check a line near the end and note how far off it is. If both are off by about the same amount, shift the subtitles here. If the gap is clearly bigger at the end, use Fix subtitle drift . For more help, read the guide Subtitles out of sync: shift vs drift . How to measure the offset The offset is the moment a line is spoken minus the time the subtitle file gives for it. Find a clear line of dialogue near the start of the video. Note the time when it is spoken, for example 00:05:12.4 . Open the subtitle file in a text editor and find the same line. Note its start time, for example 00:05:14,900 . Subtract: 00:05:12,400 − 00:05:14,900 = −2.5 seconds. Enter -2500 . Most players only show whole seconds, so your first number may be a little off. Shift once, test the result in your player, and adjust by a few hundred milliseconds if needed. What happens to lines shifted before 00:00:00 A subtitle can't start before the video does, so SubtitleFixer removes or trims lines that a negative shift pushes past 00:00:00. A line that would end at or before 00:00:00 is removed. A line ending exactly at 00:00:00,000 would have no length, so it is removed too. A line that would start before 00:00:00 but end after it starts at 00:00:00 and keeps its new end time. In an SRT file , the remaining lines are renumbered 1, 2, 3… You see a message with the number of lines removed and trimmed, so nothing disappears without you knowing. In this example the shift is -3000 ms . Line 1 is removed, line 2 is trimmed, and the rest move as usual. Before: 1 00:00:01,000 --> 00:00:02,500 (Music) 2 00:00:02,200 --> 00:00:04,800 Previously on Harbour Lights… 3 00:00:05,100 --> 00:00:07,000 You can't stay here. After shifting by -3000 ms: 1 00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:01,800 Previously on Harbour Lights… 2 00:00:02,100 --> 00:00:04,000 You can't stay here. Shift from a specific line You can shift only part of a file by entering the line number where the shift should start. In an SRT file, the line number is the cue number. In a VTT or ASS file, it is the line's position in the file, counting from 1. The shift always runs to the end of the file. This is useful when subtitles are in sync at first and then suddenly jump off, for example after an extra scene or where an ad break was cut. Lines before the one you choose keep their original times. In this example the subtitles are fine up to line 2, and from line 3 on they appear 1.2 seconds too early. The shift is +1200 ms, starting from line 3 . Before: 2 00:00:55,100 --> 00:00:57,000 Wait for me. 3 00:00:59,300 --> 00:01:01,850 We're late again. After: 2 00:00:55,100 --> 00:00:57,000 Wait for me. 3 00:01:00,500 --> 00:01:03,050 We're late again. Line 2 didn't move. Line 3 and every line after it moved 1.2 seconds later. If a later part of the file is off by a different amount, run the tool again on the fixed file, starting from that line. Player delay vs fixing the file A player's subtitle delay is temporary, while shifting the file fixes it for good. In VLC you can change the subtitle delay while watching (with the G and H keys on Windows and Linux, in 50 ms steps), but the delay only lasts while that video is open. Other players have similar settings, and they only work in that one player. A shifted subtitle file plays in sync everywhere: in any player, on your TV, and for anyone you share it with. A practical way to work is to find the right delay in your player first, then enter the same amount here. VTT to SRT converter : turn VTT captions into an SRT file. ASS to SRT converter : turn styled ASS subtitles into a plain SRT file. Guide: Subtitles out of sync: shift vs drift . FAQ How do I fix subtitles that are out of sync by the same amount? Shift the whole file by that amount. Measure how far one line is off, enter the difference in milliseconds, and download the fixed file. If the gap gets bigger as the video plays, the problem is drift, and you need Fix subtitle drift instead. Should I enter a positive or negative number? Enter a positive number if the subtitles appear too early, and a negative number if they appear too late. For example, subtitles that show up 2 seconds after the words are spoken need -2000. How do I know how many milliseconds to shift? Subtract the subtitle's start time in the file from the moment the line is actually spoken in the video. If a line is spoken at 00:05:12.4 but the file says 00:05:14,900, the result is -2.5 seconds, so you enter -2500. You can use any whole number of milliseconds, so half a second is 500. Can I shift only from a certain line onwards? Yes. Enter the number of the line where the problem starts, and SubtitleFixer shifts that line and every line after it to the end of the file, while the lines before it stay unchanged. In an SRT file this is the cue number; in a VTT or ASS file it is the line's position in the file, counting from 1. My subtitles start in sync and then drift further off. Will shifting fix it? No. Shifting moves every line by the same amount, so it can't fix a gap that keeps growing. Use Fix subtitle drift , which re-times the file from two lines you set yourself. Which formats can I shift, and does the format change? You can shift SRT, VTT and ASS files, and the format stays the same. An SRT file comes back as an SRT file, a VTT file as a VTT file, and an ASS file as an ASS file with its header and styles untouched. What's the difference between VLC's subtitle delay and fixing the file? VLC's subtitle delay only applies while that video is open in VLC, and the subtitle file itself doesn't change. Shifting the file fixes it once, so it plays in sync in any player, on your TV, and for anyone you share it with. Is my subtitle file uploaded? No. SubtitleFixer shifts your subtitles inside your browser, and the file never leaves your device. There is no upload and no sign-up.

Drag one or more .srt files onto the page, or click to choose them. Convert. SubtitleFixer turns each SRT file into a WebVTT (.vtt) file with the same text and timings. Download. One file downloads as a VTT file; several files download together as one zip. Example: before and after The conversion adds a WEBVTT header, removes the cue numbers and changes the comma in each timestamp to a period. Before (SRT file): 1 00:00:01,200 --> 00:00:03,800 Hi, and welcome back. 2 00:00:04,100 --> 00:00:07,450 Today we're fixing subtitles. After (VTT file): WEBVTT 00:00:01.200 --> 00:00:03.800 Hi, and welcome back. 00:00:04.100 --> 00:00:07.450 Today we're fixing subtitles. The times are exactly the same: 00:00:01,200 became 00:00:01.200 . The text didn't change, and the cue numbers are gone because VTT doesn't need them. What it does and doesn't do The converter changes the file format from SRT to VTT. It does not change the text or the timing. What it does: Converts SubRip (.srt) subtitles to WebVTT (.vtt). Adds the WEBVTT header, removes the cue numbers and uses the VTT timestamp format. Keeps italic, bold and underline tags ( <i> , <b> , <u> ). Detects the SRT file's encoding and saves the VTT file as UTF-8. Tick "Add BOM (old players)" if your device needs a BOM. Keeps every start and end time exactly, to the millisecond. Converts many SRT files at once, with one zip to download. Runs in your browser: your files never leave your device, and there's no sign-up. What it doesn't do: It doesn't repair double-encoded text like Ã© . If your SRT file already shows garbled characters, fix it first with Fix subtitle encoding , then convert. It doesn't fix subtitles that are out of sync. Use Shift subtitles for that. It doesn't add styling or positioning. SRT files don't contain VTT positioning, so there is nothing to carry over. It doesn't convert VTT back to SRT. For that, use the VTT to SRT converter . What changes between SRT and VTT SRT and VTT store almost the same information, so converting SRT to VTT only changes a few small things. Header: a VTT file starts with the line WEBVTT . SRT files have no header. Timestamps: SRT uses a comma before the milliseconds ( 00:00:01,200 ), VTT uses a period ( 00:00:01.200 ). Line numbers: SRT needs a number above each subtitle. In VTT these numbers are optional, so SubtitleFixer leaves them out. Tags: <i> , <b> and <u> work in both formats and are kept as they are. For a full comparison of the formats, read SRT vs VTT vs ASS . How to add a VTT file to an HTML5 video To show VTT subtitles on a web page, add a <track> element inside the <video> element. <video controls src="movie.mp4"> <track kind="subtitles" src="movie.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default> </video> If the subtitles don't appear: Check that the src of the track points to the right .vtt file. Make sure your server sends .vtt files with the content type text/vtt . If the .vtt file is on a different domain from the page, the server must allow it (CORS), and the <video> element needs a crossorigin attribute. Test the page through a web server, not by opening it from your disk ( file:// ). Some browsers block subtitle tracks on local files. Both are plain-text subtitle formats with a timestamp and text for each line. VTT (WebVTT) is the format HTML5 video players in web browsers use, and it adds a header, a slightly different timestamp format and optional styling and positioning. Can I just rename an .srt file to .vtt? No. A VTT file must start with the line WEBVTT and use a period instead of a comma before the milliseconds, so web browsers reject a renamed SRT file. Converting the file on this page makes both changes for you. Will the timing, formatting or special characters change? SubtitleFixer detects your SRT file's encoding and saves the VTT file as UTF-8, which WebVTT requires. Can I convert multiple SRT files at once? Yes. The file itself is usually fine; the problem is how it is loaded. Check that the track element points to the right file, that the server sends .vtt files as text/vtt, and that the page is not opened straight from your disk (file://), which some browsers block for subtitle tracks. txt-to-srt.html: How to convert TXT to SRT in 3 steps You can turn text into a subtitle file in three steps, and your text stays on your device the whole time. Add your text. Paste it into the box, or drag a .txt file onto the page. Choose a mode. Pick "Plain text" if your text has no times, or "Text with timestamps" if it already has them. Check the start time and reading speed if you need to. Download. Save the result as an SRT file, or switch the output to VTT. The timings are estimated from your text, not from the audio of your video. If the subtitles need to match the speech exactly, see Matching the subtitles to your video below. Example: plain text Every line of text becomes one subtitle. At the default reading speed of 17 characters per second, a line of 21 characters stays on screen for about 1.2 seconds. Before (text): Hi, and welcome back. Today we're fixing subtitles. First, open your file. After (SRT file): 1 00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:01,235 Hi, and welcome back. 2 00:00:01,235 --> 00:00:02,941 Today we're fixing subtitles. 3 00:00:02,941 --> 00:00:04,235 First, open your file. Each subtitle starts when the previous one ends. Set a gap in milliseconds if you want a short pause between them, or a start time if the speech doesn't begin at 00:00:00. Example: text with timestamps If your text already has times, such as a transcript copied from YouTube, SubtitleFixer keeps them. Before (text): 0:00 Hi, and welcome back. 0:04 Today we're fixing subtitles. 0:09 First, open your file. After (SRT file): 1 00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:04,000 Hi, and welcome back. 2 00:00:04,000 --> 00:00:09,000 Today we're fixing subtitles. 3 00:00:09,000 --> 00:00:10,294 First, open your file. Each subtitle ends when the next one starts. The last one has no next line, so its length comes from the reading speed. These timestamp styles are recognised: 00:01:05 text [00:01:05] text 1:05 text , as in a YouTube transcript 00:01:05,200 --> 00:01:07,000 on its own line, with the text below it Settings Plain text mode has a few settings, and all of them have sensible defaults. Split by: lines (default) or sentences. With sentences, each sentence becomes its own subtitle, even when several are on one line. Lines are never joined, so a sentence that runs onto the next line becomes two subtitles. Start time: when the first subtitle appears, as hh:mm:ss,mmm . Default: 00:00:00,000 . Reading speed: characters per second. Default: 17. Minimum and maximum duration: how short or long one subtitle can be. Default: 1 to 7 seconds. Gap: a pause between subtitles, in milliseconds. Default: 0. Fit to total duration: enter the length of your video, and the timings are stretched or squeezed to fill it, with longer lines getting more time. The minimum and maximum duration don't apply in this case. Lines longer than 42 characters are split into subtitles of up to two lines each. In "Text with timestamps" mode, Start time and Gap aren't used, because the times come from your text. What it does and doesn't do The converter turns text into a subtitle file. It doesn't change your words. What it does: Turns plain text into SRT subtitles, one line or one sentence per subtitle. Times each subtitle by reading speed, or keeps the timestamps already in your text. Splits long lines into subtitles of up to two lines. Saves as SRT or VTT. Detects the encoding of your .txt file, so Cyrillic, Arabic or Chinese text reads correctly, and saves the result as UTF-8. Tick "Add BOM (old players)" if your player or TV needs a BOM. Runs in your browser: your text never leaves your device, and there's no sign-up. What it doesn't do: It doesn't listen to audio or video. It can't transcribe speech or line the text up with it. It doesn't translate the text. It doesn't burn subtitles into a video. It creates a separate subtitle file that you load in your player or video editor. Matching the subtitles to your video Timings from reading speed are a starting point, and they rarely match the speech exactly. Here's how to get closer. Set the start time (in "Plain text" mode) to the moment the first line is spoken, so the whole file starts in the right place. Use timestamps if you have them. A transcript with times, from YouTube or a transcription tool, gives far better timings than reading speed. Fix the rest in the file. If every subtitle is early or late by the same amount, use Shift subtitles . If the gap grows towards the end, set the correct time for two lines with Fix subtitle drift . Related tools SRT to TXT : turn subtitles back into plain text. Shift subtitles : move every subtitle earlier or later. Fix subtitle drift : re-time subtitles that slowly go out of sync. SRT to VTT converter : turn SRT subtitles into VTT for web video players. Guide: Subtitles out of sync: shift vs drift . Fix subtitle encoding FAQ How do I convert a text file to SRT? Paste the text or drop the .txt file on this page, choose "Plain text" or "Text with timestamps", and download the SRT file. Each line of text becomes one subtitle, and everything happens in your browser with no upload. How are the timings calculated? In "Plain text" mode, each subtitle stays on screen long enough to read it: 17 characters per second by default, at least 1 second and at most 7 seconds. The first subtitle starts at the start time you set, and each next one starts when the previous one ends. You can change all of these settings. With "Fit to total duration" on, the minimum and maximum don't apply: the total time is shared out by the number of characters in each subtitle. Can it sync the text to my video's audio? No. SubtitleFixer doesn't listen to the audio, so the timings are estimated from the length of the text. To match the speech, turn the audio into a transcript with timestamps first (for example with a transcription tool), then use "Text with timestamps" mode, or adjust the result with Shift subtitles and Fix subtitle drift . How do I turn a YouTube transcript into SRT? Copy the transcript with its timestamps, paste it here and choose "Text with timestamps". Lines like 1:05 text keep their start times, and each subtitle ends when the next one starts. How long should one subtitle be? A common rule is at most two lines of about 42 characters each, which is what the Netflix style guide for English sets. SubtitleFixer splits longer lines into subtitles of that size. The default reading speed of 17 characters per second is the limit Netflix uses for children's programs, so it is comfortable to read; Netflix allows up to 20 for adult programs. Can I make an SRT file for song lyrics? Yes. Put one lyric line on each line of text. If you know when each line is sung, add the times in front of the lines and use "Text with timestamps", because reading speed alone won't match the music. Can I get a VTT file instead of SRT? Yes.
